items.title: This week Sony revived its classic Walkman headphones
items.summary:
This week on Dezeen , Japanese electronics company Sony launched a remake of its original Walkman headphones , which have colourful foam pads and lean into 1980s nostalgia.

The headphones, called MDR-3R, resemble the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979. However, the new edition has a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices.

Gustaf Westman's full Disney collection has been revealed 

Other design news included Swedish designer Gustaf Westman's unveiling of his full collection for media company Disney , including a bookstand shaped like Donald Duck and a mirror that resembles Pluto.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” Westman told Dezeen about working with the familiar characters. 

A watch by Steven Holl was revealed with colourful raised blocks 

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny informed by a compliment architect Álvaro Siza once gave him, telling Holl he used colour "like Matisse".

The colourful watch, which has a three-dimensional dial with red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks, was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects.

The La Querola housing development was damaged in a fire 

A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire .

Called La Querola, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s…
items.t: This week Sony revived its classic Walkman headphones

items.title: The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper
items.summary:
For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

But what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style , found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper. 

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

“It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S . For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

Giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro , is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more…
items.t: The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper

items.title: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between
items.summary:
Though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison , an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

Tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

But her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”

That perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has…
items.t: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between

items.title: Cold Plunges Are Finding a New Place in Residential Design
items.summary:
Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a new place in residential design. As the wellness practice grows in popularity, homeowners are increasingly looking to incorporate cold therapy directly into their bathrooms, transforming what was once a standalone piece of fitness equipment into an integrated feature of the home.

The interest goes beyond athletic recovery. Cold-water immersion has been associated with potential benefits ranging from reduced muscle soreness to improved sleep and stress management, although research into its broader health effects remains limited. Still, the appeal is evident. According to Houzz’s 2024 Summer Trends Report , searches for “cold plunge” increased 74% year over year, while searches for “indoor sauna” rose 69%.

In the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging. Photography by Steve C. Wilson.

That interest reflects a larger shift toward wellness-focused residential spaces. The company’s 2026 report found that searches for “wellness room” had increased 164%, suggesting that homeowners are thinking more intentionally about how their environments can support relaxation and well-being.

For interior designers, these changing priorities are introducing new considerations into residential projects. Arizona-based designer Stephanie Larsen , who incorporates cold plunges, infrared saunas, and integrated aromatherapy systems into her work, has seen clients place…
items.t: Cold Plunges Are Finding a New Place in Residential Design

items.title: Ocean liner sunk in Florida to become "world's largest artificial reef"
items.summary:
On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida .

The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.

Photography 

Previous 

Next 

Photography

Close 

The ship will join a long stretch of artificial reefs , including 580 other decommissioned vessels and structures, that line the ocean floor off the coast Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.

"A new chapter has begun in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida, where the legendary SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, has completed her final voyage to become the World's Largest Artificial Reef," said a release from the government of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. 

The site serves as a tourist and dive destination for SCUBA divers both new and seasoned, as the underwater structures are meant to provide infrastructure for marine life.

"Beyond its appeal as a dive destination, the SS United States will serve an important environmental purpose," said the team. 

"Her massive structure will provide new habitat for marine life, supporting the growth of an underwater ecosystem that includes inhabitants such as sea turtles, grouper, snapper and marlin."

In preparation for its scuttling, the ship underwent a years-long remediation process , where it was stripped of toxic materials, such as green neotex exterior floor covering and paint.

Elements such as the ventilation system, wiring and the propeller were…

Located in Manhattan's SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari's fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers "the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge," according to the team.

"The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision," said Iannone.

items.title: Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture
items.summary:
French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet's, offices and a food court. 

"The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot," Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

"However, the building's footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context," it continued.

"We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa."

items.title: BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda
items.summary:
Architecture studio BIG has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by BIG in collaboration with social enterprise To.org , the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a "resilient economic model" that empowers displaced communities.

Gallery 

Previous 

Next 

Gallery

Close 

Section

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels. 

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by BIG to be "scalable and modular" to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees," Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a "fractal approach" – beginning with the establishment of housing units before…
items.t: BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda

The film is the latest in a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award's 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are shown the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion, revived by London-based Studio Octopi to bring its tea pavilion and pools fully back into use.

The studio aimed to retain the historic character of the 1930s art deco building, while introducing considered upgrades, including a marble-clad exterior.

"We wanted to pay homage to the art deco period, which the building was originally conceived in," said Studio Octopi director James Lowe.

"The green came about really in connection with the paint samples that we took off the railings, and it was decided to go with marble that would give resilience to the environment."

items.title: Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse
items.summary:
On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London's V&A East Storehouse.

The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May , has been lauded for opening up the V&A 's storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.

The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

To speak to this demographic, studio founder Robin Howie decided to borrow a visual language they're already intimately familiar with.

"We studied popular Gen-Z apps and services to understand how to make Storehouse feel intuitive as soon as you walk through the door," Howie told Dezeen.

"Cultural institutions can all too often feel like exclusive environments with many barriers to entry. It's unfortunately far too easy for so many people to walk into a museum, gallery or national organisation and feel a queasy sense of 'this isn’t really for me'."

As an antidote, Howie and his team decided to treat the wayfinding design like an operating system in itself, looking to the UX of much-used apps like TikTok to inform signage and interaction points across the museum.

From the get-go, visitors are welcomed with an "onboarding text" that introduces them to the Storehouse and how to navigate it.

"It's a moment that purposefully feels like opening an app…
items.t: Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse

items.title: Pablo Castillo partners with Decibel on 3D-printed chair with under-seat storage
items.summary:
A bookshelf slots in below the cantilevered seat of Kino, a 3D-printed chair developed by Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo.

Castillo designed Kino for Decibel , an American company that specialises in 3D-printed furniture and installations. It is shortlisted for seating design of the year in the upcoming Dezeen Awards .

The designer's aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

The chair is essentially a monobloc, with a single component forming the T-shaped seat, two legs, the shelf and a curved backrest.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

Decibal also offers an outdoor version printed from recycled PETG, a thermoplastic polyester.

"I wanted the substantial thickness of the plastic and the way it builds a product layer by layer to translate into features that give the chair its character," Castillo told Dezeen.

Read:

Gareth Neal and the New Raw develop 3D printing style based on crafts 

"Following this line of thought allowed me to move beyond mere dimensions and general ergonomic considerations," the designer said.

"The cantilevered seat, the under-seat storage, and specific details such as the T-junctions naturally emerged."

The seat's T-shape was created by cantilevers both forwards and backwards. This makes the chair less rigid than a typical 3D-printed chair, improving comfort.

"By reinforcing the lower part of the…
items.t: Pablo Castillo partners with Decibel on 3D-printed chair with under-seat storage

items.title: Finnegan Shannon installs conveyor belt for displaying art accessibly in Brooklyn
items.summary:
New York City-based artist Finnegan Shannon has installed a conveyor belt to display art at cultural centre Pioneer Works in Brooklyn , USA, as a commentary on accessibility in art.

According to Pioneer Works , the There's No Me Without You installation fulfils Shannon’s “longtime fantasy of an exhibition space that would meet their access needs”. 

Photography 

Previous 

Next 

Photography

Close 

Chairs were placed around the closed-loop 12-foot-long mechanism, letting visitors sit when viewing and engaging with exhibited objects, archival materials and portable DVD players placed on a series of moving trays. 

It was created from a restaurant-style system similar to those used in sushi restaurants where the food is delivered via a conveyor belt. The rest of the room on the upper floor of the arts centre was covered in rich fabrics and built-in benches along the perimeter. 

“My conveyor belt, technically a retail and restaurant-style display system, is a tool for me to be in less pain when I’m experiencing art,” said Shannon , who is disabled. “I notice I am a much more patient and curious visitor when I’m sitting down.”   

The title of the installation reflects the artist's relationship to the concept of interdependence.

“If disabled people were in charge, we would have a bunch of varied and deluxe options for sitting and lying down in exhibition spaces,” they said. 

“Instead we live in a world where this type of infrastructure is quite basic and sparse.” 

The installation is being used to present new commissions by artists with disabilities Joselia Rebekah…
items.t: Finnegan Shannon installs conveyor belt for displaying art accessibly in Brooklyn

items.title: Crosslam completes Brazil's tallest mass-timber tower
items.summary:
Engineering company Crosslam has designed and built Aurora 275, a hybrid building with mass-timber elements that the company claims is the tallest of its type in Brazil . 

Standing 22 metres tall, Aurora 275 is considered a hybrid-timber building, with a structural system consisting of a reinforced concrete core, metal, and mass-timber elements including glued-laminated timber (glulam) beams and columns.

Photography 

Previous 

Next 

Photography

Close 

Located in the Suzano area of São Paulo, according to Crosslam , it is the tallest building of its type in Brazil. 

Crosslam, which usually acts as an engineer for other firms, designed the building itself to demonstrate the potential of mass timber in Brazil.

"We believed that, to sell the first timber building, we first had to build our own," said Crosslam founder José Alberto Corrêa. "Otherwise, the Brazilian market wouldn't trust that it was possible."

To further demonstrate the method's viability, the building was constructed in four weeks by a five-person team, according to Crosslam. The timber was produced in the company's factory using wood sourced from Brazil. 

Aurora 275 sits next to smaller residential buildings. It features a metal-clad facade, with yellow detailing running up its face. 

It extends in two directions from a concrete core, with balconies for each of the 10 apartments. 

On the outside, the timber elements are only visible on the undersides of the balconies. 

However, on the inside, the timber elements are more visible, with the cross-laminated timber floorplates and glulam beams…
items.t: Crosslam completes Brazil's tallest mass-timber tower

items.title: ROOM’s Designers on Design Series Returns with A Story of Hospitality and Human Connection
items.summary:
Who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer? That’s the core concept behind ROOM ’s Designers on Design video series, which pairs leading designers together for open conversation on the future of architecture, design, and human connection.

“When we launched ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” says Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM. “No interviewer, no moderator, no prescribed talking points. Just two creative minds coming together to exchange ideas, challenge perspectives, and explore what moves the industry forward.”

Hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation. Designed by Neri&Hu in partnership with local architects and professional firms, the hotel draws inspiration from the site’s industrial maritime character while embracing the city’s evolving cultural landscape. Although the original warehouse was too unstable to preserve, its footprint and construction logic informed the new building, which references the long, narrow forms and pitched roofs of the surrounding industrial structures.

Photography by Jiri Lizler

Part of a global portfolio of hotels, The Cape Town Edition revolves around The Drum—a soaring cylindrical space open to the elements. The harbor, Table Mountain, the Atlantic, and the waterfront below are all visible from the 360-degree outdoor viewing platform. Guests, visitors, and locals alike can ascend the spiral staircase to discover Cape Town from a bird’s-eye view.

Photography by Jiri Lizler

For Lyndon Neri , co-founder of Neri&Hu, The Drum began with a conversation about how to connect and distinguish the hotel’s hospitality and residential spaces. “The route is both architectural and civic,” he says. “It turns circulation into an experience of the landscape and gives the project a public dimension beyond accommodation.”

items.title: 25 Years of Bilibo: The Toy That Lets Imagination Lead
items.summary:
With two round eyes and a curving grin, Bilibo looks like a character waiting for its story to begin. Designed by Swiss designer Alex Hochstrasser, the sculptural shell is an open-ended toy that can become anything from a seat or boat to a helmet or drum. Twenty-five years after its 2001 debut, the toy remains remarkably unchanged, a testament to the enduring appeal of a design that leaves almost everything to the imagination.

To mark the milestone, Moluk , the Zurich-based toy company Hochstrasser runs with his sister Doris, an architect, is introducing Bilibo Midi , a smaller shell for toddlers, and Bilibo Dots , a set of colorful counters that translate the original’s open-ended approach into a new form.

Photography courtesy of Moluk

Both additions build on the premise that has carried Bilibo into homes, classrooms, and museum collections around the world—and continues to anchor Moluk’s entire catalog: offer a pared-back object and leave the rest to the imagination.

The Toy That Lets Kids Make the Rules 
 Hochstrasser’s starting point for Bilibo was what he saw on store shelves at the turn of the millennium. “I was struck by how rigidly most mainstream toys were categorized by age and gender, giving them an expiration date long before they wore out,” he says. “There was also a flood of licensed toys, with the story already written. I wanted to create something more universal and inclusive that could grow with children and leave them in charge of the story.”

Alex Hochstrasser’s sketches for the first Bilibo. Illustration courtesy of Moluk.

items.t: 25 Years of Bilibo: The Toy That Lets Imagination Lead

items.title: Faulty Wedding Cake pavilion to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor
items.summary:
A 12-metre-high pavilion shaped like a wedding cake is set to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor in Buckinghamshire, UK , after it was closed over health and safety concerns.

A spokesperson for the Grade I-listed country house told the BBC that the pavilion , which was installed in 2023, was not "open for quite as long as hoped" due to faults in its ceramic tiles.

The sculptural pavilion, simply named Wedding Cake, was designed by Portuguese artist Joana Vasconcelos as a permanent garden pavilion for the grounds of Waddesdon Manor.

Its three tiers are wrapped in glazed, pastel-toned ceramic tiles made by the historic Portuguese tile manufacturer Viúva Lamego and intended to look like cake icing. They are now faulty, forcing the structure to close because of concerns about their safety.

A report including photos of the damaged tiles was shared on Buckinghamshire Council's online planning portal, but the root cause has not been publicly stated. 

According to the BBC, a Buckinghamshire Council officer found that no viable solution to repair the faulty tiles had been identified.

As such, the council has approved a change to the listed building consent, allowing the sculpture to be removed. As the manor and its grounds are protected sites, permission must be obtained to carry out such work.

The structure must now be removed no later than January 2036. However, the Rothschild Foundation, which manages the estate, wants the sculpture removed as soon as possible, according to the BBC. 

The revised consent also requires the surrounding landscape to be returned to grass within…
items.t: Faulty Wedding Cake pavilion to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor

items.title: Renovation delays pose "Notre Dame-like" fire risk for Houses of Parliament
items.summary:
A government report has found that risks of a major fire at the Palace of Westminster are rising as health and safety incidents increase at the UK parliament building in London , amid continuing delays to its renovation.

Released last week by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the report said that maintenance costs for the UNESCO-listed structure are expected to rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if no action is taken. According to the latest report on the restoration, the overall cost of the renovation will rise by £420 million for each year the project is delayed.

Parliament voted in 2018 to vacate the Palace for restoration, however this has been delayed by ongoing disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the anticipated decades-long renovation.

"Political allergy" to updating the building 

According to Public Accounts Committee chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, current fire risks could result in "Notre Dame-like flames" at the parliament building, which in 2023 was reported by the committee to be at "constant risk of fire".

"There has long been a political allergy to gripping the nettle that is R&R [repair and renovation]," Clifton-Brown said.

"Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building's roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life," he continued.

"These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks which our committee identified three years ago."

Renovation strategy to be decided by 2030…

British start-up Minimal has designed an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van in the Pedal 4, now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

Shortlisted in the consumer product design category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, Pedal 4 was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London's crowded and complex streets.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle has a footprint not much larger than a bike – three metres by one metre – and is able to go down pedestrianised roads and use cycle infrastructure, according to Minimal .

"Electric vans solve the emissions problem, but not the access problem," said Minimal CEO and co-founder Patrick Bion. "They still sit in the same traffic, fight for the same kerb space and need a driver with a licence."

Designed as one piece, the system allows an entire wall to be specified at once, in a range of finishes and layouts suited to a living room, a study, a bedroom, or a home office.

The idea grew from how founder and CEO Tom Hu regards the wall. “A residence is defined as much by its walls as by its furniture,” he says. “Usually, though, paneling, shelves, display cabinets, storage, and lighting are specified separately and added to the wall one by one, and the wall becomes a place where many decisions meet but never quite agree.” Canvas brings them together from the start, in the same design language as the rest of Arundel.

Material Range 
 Panels come in layered or plain walnut grain or a pale oak grain, and the frame in matte black, espresso brown, graphite grey, or satin platinum. The display cabinets take one of four types of glass, among them clear and frosted, and the console top comes in two tones. “The structure stays exactly the same; the character changes completely,” Hu explains. “Walnut grain with a dark frame and grey glass makes a warm, low-lit library for the evening. items.title: Licht Kunst Licht illuminates Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade with "largely invisible" lights
items.summary:
Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht has used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world's tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

Licht Kunst Licht (LKL) collaborated with RheinEnergie and the Dombauhütte Köln restoration workshop to develop a lighting concept for Cologne 's historic cathedral, which is also Germany’s most visited landmark. 

Prior to the intervention, it was primarily illuminated using floodlights placed atop nearby buildings. These 1,000-watt metal halide lamps consumed a great deal of energy and, according to LKL, flooded the building in an unflattering neutral white light.

LKL replaced this broad-brush approach with discreet, warm-spectrum LED fixtures, illuminating the building’s Gothic features by providing subtle backlighting combined with vertical grazing light to enliven the ornate facades.

“The central concept ‘light follows architecture’ replaces indiscriminate floodlighting with targeted illumination,” the studio explained. 

“Instead of flattening the facade, light is directed to articulate depth, rhythm and verticality. The outcome is a sculptural night presence while the luminaires remain largely invisible by day.”

The project’s key innovation was the development of bespoke, multifunctional lighting poles that are covertly integrated into the structure using custom clamps to protect the stonework. The aim was to render the fixtures "largely invisible" during the day and allow them to be dismantled without impacting the historic structure.

items.title: Reviving an Enduring Emblem of Simplicity, Loll Designs Launches the Here and There Collection
items.summary:
The best designs almost always come out of necessity and quiet observation. In the 1940s, legendary ecologist Aldo Leopold constructed a remarkably straightforward wooden bench so that he could sit outside his Wisconsin farmstead and contemplate nature’s primal force; the fundamental need for its conservation. The back-slanted seat was constructed from readily available dimensional lumber and almost immediately presented itself as an act of unpretentious, serendipitous genius: the quick assembly of a functional furnishing devised for a specific need but ultimately, one with universal potential. The particular brilliance of the design was its x-shaped self-bracing geometry, zero waste configuration, and uncomplicated assembly.

“Anyone that’s handy with a saw and some fasteners and lumber could easily build an Aldo bench,” says Eric Swanson, president of Duluth-based outdoor furniture brand Loll Designs. “That’s the beauty of it.” The Minnesota manufacturer recently teamed up with Michigan industrial design studio Argenta Park to turn the foundational artifact into the Here and There Collection. Named for Leopold’s belief that our appreciation for the natural world should balance between what’s nearby and farther afield, the cohesive and complementary suite of furnishings includes a dining chair, dining table, and of course, a bench.

Photography courtesy of Loll Designs.

This contemporary reinterpretation was twelve years in the making. For his outdoor wedding in 2014, Argenta Park designer Ricky Biddle was faced with the same practical challenge Leopold surmounted…

Danny Kaplan designed the Paravent Bed for his own home, basing its strong, paneled silhouette on the hinged screens of Jean-Michel Frank, before he and Vince Patti of Lesser Miracle saw the potential for a larger commercial collection. That collection launched in 2024. Following its commercial success, the two New York–based designers have expanded it with Delf II , adding a desk, a coffee table, a console, and a nightstand that extend the series beyond the bedroom.

Photography by Brent Goldsmith

The relationship between wood and ceramic remains central to the collection. Each piece is crafted from white oak and accented with hand-built ceramic, the pairing that defined the original bed and inspired the collection’s name. Delf derives from delven , the Dutch verb meaning to mine or to dig, a reference to the channels carved into the wood and filled by hand with ceramic tile inlays.

Photography by Brent Goldsmith

Kaplan, a self-taught ceramicist who founded his studio in 2015, creates the tilework, drawing inspiration from the pottery of Vallauris, a region in southern France known for its ceramics. It is offered in the studio’s signature glazes: Stone, Anthracite, Terrasig, Ivy, Lapis, Agate, Bronze, and Chestnut, along with a new Navy. items.title: Monopoly and Scrabble Get a Scandinavian Modern Redesign
items.summary:
Monopoly and Scrabble have been fixtures of family game nights for generations, but their colorful boards and familiar pieces rarely stay out once the competition ends. When the last property has been traded or the final word spelled, everything usually disappears back into a cabinet. WS Game Company is rethinking that relationship between play and display.

The new Nordic Collection gives the two classic board games a Scandinavian-inspired redesign, replacing conventional folding boards and cardboard boxes with warm wood, understated graphics, and carefully considered details. Launched last month, the collection draws on the principles of Scandinavian modernism to create games that feel as much like design objects as they do as games.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company

“The Nordic Collection was inspired by the rich design history of Scandinavian modern design,” explains Kerry Addis, co-owner and COO of WS Game Company. She points to designers such as Hans Wegner and Arne Jacobsen, who combined natural materials and traditional craftsmanship with modern production techniques to create objects that were both innovative and inviting. For the Nordic Collection, the goal was to bring that same balance of familiarity and innovation to the games’ form, construction, and functionality.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company

The goal was to create something that could fit comfortably into an existing interior while offering meaningful innovations in form, construction, and practicality.

items.title: How Mannington Commercial Approaches Design as a System
items.summary:
Family-owned flooring manufacturer Mannington Commercial aims to solve problems for interior designers and their clients. That’s why the company focuses on giving designers more freedom and flexibility with product, as discussed in The Art of Versatility last year. Building on that concept, Mannington Commercial designs products in families so individual flooring collections work together across an entire project.

“An entryway has different demands than a lobby, patient room, corridor, or collaborative area, but those spaces still need to feel connected. If every collection lives on its own island, then the designer has to create all of those relationships,” says Stacey Gerbman, Mannington Commercial Director of Design. “The shift is from thinking only about individual launches to thinking about the life of the entire portfolio.”

Rather than creating matching sets, Mannington Commercial establishes a design language that allows products to complement one another and carry a design concept throughout a project. Each new product should be distinct yet work with existing and future collections, simplifying specification for interior designers.

Stepping Stones. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Mannington Commercial’s design team plans ahead to ensure new collections pair naturally with existing lines. “Before a collection is fully developed, we look at the portfolio as a whole: where there are gaps, which colors and undertones are important, what scales are missing, and which materials the new collection is likely to sit beside,” says Gerbman. items.title: The laundry miracle: how to solve 10 stubborn problems – from stains to rough towels to ‘permastank’
items.summary:
For 1 million people on Reddit, the science of clothes-washing is a regular topic of discussion. I tried out their tips and discovered some simple, sustainable answers

It started with a sunscreen stain – a yellowed collar on a white T-shirt that persisted wash after wash. A spray of stain remover did nothing; drying the shirt in the sun made it worse. An internet rabbit hole took me to the r/laundry subreddit, where I found my people: 995,000 of them, nerding out over the chemistry of clothes-washing.

“People want to take better care of their stuff, but don’t have the knowledge,” says Eric Thompson, a former management consultant based near Seattle who moderates the forum under the name KismaiAesthetics. He took on the mantle after seeing someone suggest white vinegar to treat a burrito stain on an anorak. “If you pour vinegar on a burrito grease stain on white nylon, you now have orange nylon for eternity,” he says. “Acids bind colour to dye sites on nylon.”

You don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15%.

However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing more of us to remain sedentary for long periods. That is where walking pads come in, being lighter, smaller and often easier to store than bulky and tricky-to-manoeuvre running treadmills.

items.title: The 10 best bean-to-cup coffee machines in the UK, tried and tested
items.summary:
Fancy an at-home coffee maker that can grind beans and make tasty espresso? Our expert put 14 to the test, including fully automatic and assisted models

• The best coffee machine for your home

Laziness is akin to godliness. I know this for a fact because, every morning, my kitchen hosts a dishevelled re-enactment of Michelangelo’s famed fresco, the Creazione di Adamo (Creation of Adam). An outstretched arm extends a single finger, and lo – a bean-to-cup machine stirs, a grinder whirs, the smell of freshly ground coffee wafts, coffee drips and milk froths. Hopefully, my cup does not runneth over, for all the big mugs are in the dishwasher.

At its simplest, this is the appeal of a fully automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine. Turn it on, place a cup on the drip tray and lazily prod a button. The machine then freshly grinds the beans, brews the coffee and – if it has an automatic milk frother – optionally adds a layer of hot frothy milk to your beverage. Your role in the process is simple: decide whether you want an espresso, lungo, americano, cappuccino, macchiato, latte or cortado. Decisions, decisions.
